facts.text: A fish stock is a population of one species of fish that shares an area and similar growth and death rates.
A stock is overexploited when the catch is larger than the maximum sustainable yield, the amount the population can replace by breeding and growing.
The data cover only assessed stocks; many fish stocks in Africa, Asia and South America have not been assessed.
FAO released its Review of the state of world marine fishery resources in June 2025 at the UN Ocean Conference; it assessed 2,570 individual stocks with more than 650 experts from over 90 countries.
The 2025 review found that 64.5 percent of stocks were fished within biologically sustainable levels and 35.5 percent were overfished.
Weighted by how much fish each stock produces, 77.2 percent of global fisheries landings came from sustainable stocks.
For tuna and tuna-like species, 87 percent of stocks were sustainable, and these stocks provided 99 percent of tuna landings.
In the Northeast Pacific, 92.7 percent of stocks were sustainable; in the Mediterranean and Black Sea, only 35.1 percent were.
In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, fishing pressure has fallen by 30 percent and fish biomass has risen by 15 percent since 2013.
FAO's Director-General said that effective management is the strongest tool for conserving fishery resources.
Derived from the dataset: the overexploited share was 10.0 percent in 1974 and 35.5 percent in 2021, about 3.55 times as high; it fell from 33.0 percent in 2008 to 32.0 percent in 2013.

Derived from the dataset: the sustainable share fell by 17.2 points between 1974 (90.0) and 2000 (72.8); the overexploited share rose by 4.8 points from 1980 to 1990, 9.1 points from 1990 to 2000 and 5.8 points from 2000 to 2008.
